# Adjudication Task — Chapter 953

## Korean source

```text
  1|＃953화
  2|
  3|
  4|
  5|수십, 수백 명이 얽혀 싸우면 전투다.
  6|
  7|하지만 그 단위가 수천, 수만으로 변한다면 그것은 더 이상 전투라고 부를 수 없다.
  8|
  9|그건 전쟁이다.
 10|
 11|서로가 온 힘을 다해 부딪치는, 각자의 모든 것을 건 전쟁.
 12|
 13|그리고 진위경은 단 한 번의 도박으로 가진 것을 모두 잃을 생각 따위는 추호도 없었다.
 14|
 15|“진천대주 진무경. 소가주께 보고드립니다.”
 16|
 17|담담한 목소리와는 달리 핏물에 흠뻑 젖은 전신.
 18|
 19|정오에 떠나 자정 무렵이 되어서야 되돌아온 진무경의 모습은, 그야말로 혈귀(血鬼)나 다름없었다.
 20|
 21|진천검이라는 별호에서 비롯된 그의 수하들 역시도.
 22|
 23|그러나 그들의 당당한 걸음걸이와 형형한 안광은, 태원진가가 거둔 첫 번째 승리의 증거였다.
 24|
 25|“지엄하신 명령에 따라, 적의 예봉을 꺾고 돌아왔나이다.”
 26|
 27|진무경은 천천히 말을 이었다.
 28|
 29|이백여 명의 진천대 중 죽은 이가 스물셋, 크고 작은 부상을 입은 이가 서른일곱.
 30|
 31|태원진가가 진룡대와 더불어 가장 심혈을 기울여 키워 낸 정예 무력대에서 단 한 번의 전투로 육십 명의 사상자가 나왔다는 소식에 몇몇 수뇌부의 낯빛이 무거워졌으나, 뒤이어 흘러나온 보고는 찰나의 슬픔마저 깨끗이 씻어냈다.
 32|
 33|일천.
 34|
 35|무려 다섯 배에 달하는 적의 선봉대를 궤멸시켰다.
 36|
 37|심지어 그중에는, 적들의 정예 병력 일백 역시 포함되어 있었다.
 38|
 39|“와아아아아!”
 40|
 41|숨죽여 상황을 듣고 있던 이들이 일제히 함성을 내질렀다.
 42|
 43|적들을 상대로 거둔 첫 번째 승리.
 44|
 45|그것도 부정할 여지조차 없는 대승(大勝).
 46|
 47|하지만 뜨겁게 달아오르는 공기 속, 진위경은 기뻐하는 와중에도 평정심을 잃지 않았다.
 48|
 49|‘이건 단지 시작에 불과하다.’
 50|
 51|그는 알고 있었다.
 52|
 53|전쟁은 하나의 모래성을 쌓는 것과 같다. 여러 번 계속해서 모래를 퍼 올려 쌓아야 완성된다.
 54|
 55|또한 그렇게 정성 들여 쌓아 올린 모래성 역시, 강한 발길질 한 번에 무너질 수 있었다.
 56|
 57|‘하지만…… 발길질에도 무너지지 않을 만큼 공고히 쌓는다면 이야기는 달라진다.’
 58|
 59|다행히 태원진가의 준비는 촉박했던 시간이 무색할 만큼 철저했다.
 60|
 61|아마도 지금쯤 장성을 넘어 산서성 북부를 지나고 있을 초원의 군세는 당혹감을 느끼고 있을 것이다.
 62|
 63|최정예가 포함되어 있던 선봉대의 전멸 소식에 한 번.
 64|
 65|그리고 정말 ‘텅 비어 버린’ 북부의 상황에 또다시 한번.
 66|
 67|‘네놈들이 북부에서 취할 수 있는 것은, 아무것도 없을 것이다.’
 68|
 69|북부에서 빠져나간 것은 사람뿐만이 아니다.
 70|
 71|진위경은 모든 병력과 양민들을 북부에서 후퇴시키는 한편, 곧 추수 시기에 이르는 논밭을 모조리 불태웠다.
 72|
 73|이른바 초토화 작전.
 74|
 75|당연히 물경 수만을 아우르는 대군을 상대로 펼치기에는 더할 나위 없는 묘수였으나, 진위경은 이 결정을 내리기 전 수십 번이나 고민했다.
 76|
 77|산서성 도지휘첨사 이풍과 수백여 명의 사람들이 먼저 그를 찾아오기 전까지는.
 78|
 79|
 80|
 81|‘비축되어 있는 군량만 수만 석입니다. 저들의 식량 문제는 충분히 감당할 수 있습니다.’
 82|
 83|
 84|
 85|주표와 홍진의 부재로 현 산서성부의 실질적 최고위 인사라 할 수 있는 이풍은 적극적인 협조를 약속했고.
 86|
 87|
 88|
 89|‘까짓거, 싹 다 불태우십쇼.’
 90|
 91|
 92|
 93|하루아침에 고향 땅을 떠나야 했던 북부의 양민들. 아니 촌장들은 이미 분노로 눈이 반쯤 뒤집힌 상태였다.
 94|
 95|
 96|
 97|‘염병할 새끼들. 허구헌날 쳐들어와서 지랄병을 떨더니 이제는 우리 논밭까지 털어먹으려고 들어?’
 98|
 99|‘이미 우리 마을 사람들도 동의했습니다. 오랑캐 놈들 주둥이로 쌀 한 톨이라도 들어갔다간 내가 찢겨 죽을 판입니다.’
100|
101|‘차라리 소나 돼지한테 쌀밥을 처먹이고 말지, 내 눈에 흙이 들어가도 그 꼴은 못 보겠소!’
102|
103|‘시바 거. 반대하는 놈 있으면 지금 나와. 누군지는 몰라도 입 벙긋했다간 오랑캐 새끼로 간주하고 머리털을 싹 밀어서 변발을 틀어 줄라니까.’
104|
105|‘거기 송 씨! 왜 아무 말도 안 해? 논밭에 꿀 발라 놨어?’
106|
107|
108|
109|그리고 한마디도 하지 않은 채 침묵을 하고 있던 송 씨 촌장은, 단 한 마디로 모두의 박수갈채를 받았다.
110|
111|
112|
113|‘불만 지르지 말고, 우물에 독을 탑시다.’
114|
115|‘……!’
116|
117|‘개울가에 똥오줌도 한 번씩 갈기고 떠나면 더 좋고.’
118|
119|‘또, 똥오줌은 왜?’
120|
121|‘물이 더러워지잖소. 똥오줌 섞인 물을 시원하게 들이키고 나면 그놈들 몸뚱어리가 멀쩡하겠소?’
122|
123|‘허어어, 어떻게 그런 묘책을……!’
124|
125|‘내가 한 번 먹어 봤어. 한 됫박 마셨다가 뒈지는 줄 알았소.’
126|
127|
128|
129|똥물 섭취라는 특이 이력을 보유한 농사꾼 송 씨는 일약 영웅으로 등극했고, 사람들은 우물에 독초를 쑤셔 박고 개울가에 똥오줌을 갈기며 왜 그가 장원 급제자 출신이 아닌지 의문을 품었다.
130|
131|착한 오랑캐는 죽은 오랑캐뿐이라는, 누군가가 들었다면 깜짝 놀랐을 이야기를 하면서.
132|
133|‘이곳까지 오는 길이, 결코 순탄치는 않을 것이다.’
134|
135|진위경은 서늘한 미소를 머금었다.
136|
137|산서성은 부정할 수 없는 변방이다.
138|
139|곡물 생산량은 상당하지만 중원만큼 발달하지도, 그만큼 강한 전력을 지닌 것도 아니다.
140|
141|하지만 그렇기에, 위기 앞에서 더욱 강하게 뭉칠 수 있다.
142|
143|오랫동안 지속된 마적단과 유목민들의 약탈은 산서인들에게 강한 심지를 심어주었고, 현재에 이르러서는 그 심지에 불이 붙었다.
144|
145|‘반드시 지켜 낸다.’
146|
147|진위경은 이미 굳게 다짐했다.
148|
149|잠과 휴식을 없애고 모든 것에 전념했다. 발 빠른 수하들을 풀어 북부의 상황을 살피고, 소규모 별동대를 꾸려 혹시 모를 병력의 분산을 파악했다.
150|
151|정양을 제외한 모든 우회로에 온갖 함정과 철질려(鐵蒺藜)를 설치한 것도, 직접 명령한 작업의 진행도를 살피는 것도 그 일환이었다.
152|
153|“토성(土城)의 진행 상황은 어찌 되어 가고 있습니까?”
154|
155|“보강 작업까지 생각한다면, 늦어도 한나절 안에는 완성될 것입니다.”
156|
157|팔천협(八天峽).
158|
159|과거 정마대전부터 지금까지, 무수한 생명을 집어삼킨 항아리 모양의 협곡 끝자락에는 지금껏 없었던 다섯 개의 성루(城樓)가 우뚝 서 있었다.
160|
161|진흙과 나무, 그리고 돌을 섞어 만든 그것의 높이는 삼 장에 달했고, 각각 이백여 명의 사람을 수용할 수 있을 만큼 평평한 면적을 지니고 있었다.
162|
163|정확히는, 이백의 궁수를.
164|
165|“협곡 위를 점령한 것만으로는 아직 부족합니다. 승리를 위해서는 반드시 필요한 일이니, 부디 토성이 무너지지 않도록 최대한 힘써 주십시오.”
166|
167|“물론입죠.”
168|
169|진위경의 당부에, 늙은 목수가 구수한 어투로 대답했다.
170|
171|짧은 대화를 나누는 두 사람의 주위에는 지금 이 순간에도 수많은 사람들이 각자 맡은 임무에 따라 움직이고 있었다.
172|
173|그들의 면면은 다양했다.
174|
175|소속된 문파 명이 새겨진 무복(武服)을 걸친 무림인들은 쉼 없이 병장기와 여러 무거운 자재를 실어 나르고, 관복 차림의 관군들은 여러 장수의 명령에 따라 일사불란하게 움직인다.
176|
177|그러나 진위경의 시선은, 소속을 알아볼 수 없을 만큼 제각각 다른 차림새로 작업에 매진하는 또 다른 이들을 향하고 있었다.
178|
179|“셋 하면 당겨!”
180|
181|“하나, 두울!”
182|
183|“흐아아압!”
184|
185|흙먼지를 뒤집어쓴 채, 연신 구슬땀을 흘리며 고된 노동을 이어 가는 사내들.
186|
187|“이 화살들은 어디에 놓죠?”
188|
189|“기름, 기름은 여기로 가져와요!”
190|
191|전투에 필요한 여러 물건들을 옮기고, 간단한 요깃거리를 준비하는 여인들.
192|
193|무려 수천여 명에 이르는 양민들을 바라보는 진위경은 가슴 한구석이 먹먹해지는 것을 느꼈다.
194|
195|‘최대한 멀리 피신하라 했거늘.’
196|
197|몇 번이나 진심을 다해 경고했다. 그리고 설득했다.
198|
199|이건 단순히 무림인들 간의 분쟁이 아니라고.
200|
201|수많은 목숨을 앗아 갈 참혹한 전쟁이며, 힘없는 그대들이 가장 큰 피해를 입을 것이라고.
202|
203|하지만 이미 마음을 정한 이들은 끝끝내 떠나지 않았다.
204|
205|곧 피바람이 휘몰아칠 전장으로 나와서까지 그들을 돕고 있었다.
206|
207|눈앞의 늙은 목수처럼.
208|
209|“우리 소가주님께서 고민이 많으신가 봅니다그려.”
210|
211|진태경을 곁눈질하던 늙은 목수가 허허 웃었다.
212|
213|몇 해 전 칠순을 넘겼다는 그가 소리 내어 웃자 절반밖에 남지 않은 이빨들 사이로 바람 소리가 새어 나왔다.
214|
215|“신경 쓰실 것 없습니다요. 이 늙은이도 그렇고, 저 사람들도 나름대로 각오하고 온 것이니.”
216|
217|“아무리 그래도…… 어찌 걱정이 안 되겠습니까.”
218|
219|“어이고, 부디 말씀 낮추십시오. 제가 살날이 얼마 남지 않은 늙은이라지만, 소가주님께 존대를 받을 정도로 염치 없진 않습니다.”
220|
221|늙은 목수가 황급히 손을 내저었다. 진위경을 바라보는 그의 회백색 눈동자에는 따뜻한 온기가 서려 있었다.
222|
223|“말 못 하는 짐승도 은혜를 입으면 언젠가는 반드시 보답하는 법입니다. 하물며 사람이라면 어찌 이런 상황을 외면할 수 있겠습니까요.”
224|
225|“그게 무슨…….”
226|
227|“이 늙은이가 한창 펄펄 날아다닐 때, 나라에 망조가 들었는지 마교인지 마구니인지 하는 잡것들이 사방을 들쑤시더니, 곧장 흉년(凶年)이 몇 해나 이어졌지요.”
228|
229|오래전의 이야기다.
230|
231|진위경이 세상에 태어나기도 전에 있었던.
232|
233|하지만 늙은 목수는 똑똑히 기억하고 있었다. 가죽을 삶아 먹고, 나무껍질을 벗겨 씹던 그 시절을.
234|
235|모두가 굶주렸기에 누군가의 도움을 바랄 수도 없었고, 도울 수도 없었던 시기.
236|
237|만약 뙤약볕이 내리쬐던 어느 날, 마을을 찾아온 한 무리의 사내들이 아니었다면 그와 가족들은 얼마 지나지 않아 굶어 죽고 말았을 것이다.
238|
239|
240|
241|‘여기가 홍가촌인가?’
242|
243|‘마, 맞습니다만. 어쩐 일로…….’
244|
245|‘후우. 다행히 제대로 찾았군.’
246|
247|
248|
249|알곡 하나 나지 않는 논밭을 일구어서 무엇 한단 말인가.
250|
251|이미 황폐한 땅을 버리고 산속으로 들어가 화전민이 된 지 오래.
252|
253|그렇기에 처음에는 도적인 줄 알았다.
254|
255|혹은 철전 하나, 알곡 한 움큼 없는 그들의 마지막 고혈을 쥐어짜기 위해 높으신 분이 보낸 장정들인 줄 알았다.
256|
257|그렇지 않고서야 이 깊은 산속까지 찾아올 이유가 없으니까.
258|
259|그러나 그들은 허리춤에 찬 검을 뽑는 대신, 제각각 짊어지고 있던 것을 내려놓았다.
260|
261|그건 커다란 자루였다.
262|
263|언제 마지막으로 보았는지 기억조차 흐릿한, 곡식과 고기가 한가득 담겨 있던 수십여 개의 자루들.
264|
265|
266|

He had ordered traps and iron caltrops set along every detour except Jeongyang. Checking the progress of the work himself was part of that effort.

[P67]
“How is the earthen fort coming along?”

[P68]
“With the reinforcement work included, it should be finished within half a day at the latest.”

[P69]
Eight Spring Gorge.

[P70]
At the far end of the vase-shaped gorge, which had swallowed countless lives from the Great Faction War to the present day, stood five towers where none had stood before.

[P71]
Built of mud, wood, and stone, each rose three *jang* high. Each had a level platform large enough to hold a little over two hundred people.

[P72]
Two hundred archers, to be exact.

[P73]
“Taking the heights above the gorge isn’t enough. These forts are essential to victory. Please do everything you can to make sure they don’t collapse.”

[P74]
“Of course, sir.”

[P75]
The old carpenter answered in a folksy drawl.

[P76]
Even as the two spoke, countless people around them went about their assigned tasks.

[P77]
They came from all walks of life.

[P78]
Martial artists in uniforms bearing the names of their sects hauled weapons and heavy materials without pause. Government troops in official uniforms moved at their officers’ commands.

[P79]
But Wikyung’s gaze settled on another group, people dressed in all sorts of clothes with no affiliation to mark them, working just as hard.

[P80]
“Pull on three!”

[P81]
“One, twooo!”

[P82]
“Hyaah!”

[P83]
Men covered in dust kept up the grueling labor, sweat pouring off them.

[P84]
“Where should we put these arrows?”

[P85]
“Oil! Bring the oil over here!”

[P86]
Women carried supplies for the battle and prepared simple food.

[P87]
Looking at the thousands of commoners, Wikyung felt a tightness in his chest.

[P88]
*I told them to flee as far away as they could.*

[P89]
He had warned them sincerely, again and again. He had tried to persuade them.

[P90]
This wasn’t merely a dispute among martial artists.

[P91]
It was a brutal war that would claim countless lives, and they, with no strength to defend themselves, would suffer the most.

[P92]
But they had made up their minds and refused to leave.

[P93]
They had even come to help here, on a battlefield that would soon be swept by bloodshed.

[P94]
Like the old carpenter standing before him.

[P95]
“Looks like our Lesser Family Head has a lot on his mind.”

[P96]
The old carpenter glanced sideways at Wikyung and chuckled.

[P97]
He had passed seventy several years ago. When he laughed, air whistled through the gaps between the few teeth he had left.

[P98]
“Don’t you worry about it. This old man and all those folks came knowing what we were getting into.”

[P99]
“But still… how could I not worry?”

[P100]
“Goodness, please don’t speak so formally to me. I may be an old man without much time left, but I’m not shameless enough to expect honorifics from the Lesser Family Head.”

[P101]
The old carpenter hurriedly waved his hands. Warmth shone in his pale gray eyes as he looked at Wikyung.

[P102]
“Even a beast that can’t speak will repay a kindness someday. How could people turn their backs at a time like this?”

[P103]
“What do you mean…?”

[P104]
“When I was young and full of life, you’d have thought the country was falling apart. The Demonic Cult, or demons, or whatever those wretches were, stirred up trouble everywhere. Then came years of famine.”

[P105]
It had happened long ago, before Jin Wikyung was born.

[P106]
But the old carpenter remembered it clearly: boiling leather to eat and stripping bark from trees to chew.

[P107]
Everyone was starving. There was no one they could ask for help, and no one able to give it.

[P108]
If a group of men hadn’t come to their village one day under the blazing sun, he and his family would have starved to death before long.

[P109]
*“Is this Hong Family Village?”*

[P110]
*“Y-yes, it is. What brings you here…?”*

[P111]
*“Phew. Thank goodness we found the right place.”*

[P112]
What was the point of tilling fields that yielded not a single grain?

[P113]
They had abandoned the barren land long before, gone into the mountains, and become slash-and-burn farmers.

[P114]
So at first, they had thought the newcomers were bandits.

[P115]
Or men sent by someone powerful to squeeze the last drops from people who had neither an iron coin nor a handful of grain left.

[P116]
Why else would anyone come this deep into the mountains?

[P117]
But instead of drawing the swords at their waists, the men set down the loads on their backs.

[P118]
They were huge sacks.

[P119]
Dozens of them, filled with grain and meat—the sight of which had grown so distant he could barely remember it.

[P120]
*“W-what in the world is this…?”*

[P121]
*“Get in line. We’ll hand it out in order.”*

[P122]
It felt like a dream.

[P123]
It still felt like one when everyone in the village lined up as the men instructed, and when he watched his wife and children, who had lain weak and helpless for days, eat until their bellies were full to bursting.

[P124]
Only after staring at that unbelievable sight and swallowing a mouthful of warm meat broth did he realize it was real.

[P125]
So he cried.

[P126]
No—everyone cried.

[P127]
They wept aloud even as they chewed and swallowed the food in their mouths.

[P128]
Because they wanted to live. Because they wanted to know they were alive.

[P129]
“If they hadn’t helped us that day, this old man and my family would have starved to death there.”

[P130]
The old carpenter looked at Wikyung with tears in his eyes. Unlike back then, he had a broad smile on his face.

[P131]
“But those good people tried to leave without a word. So I grabbed one of them by the leg and hung on.”

[P132]
He couldn’t read, not even the writing on their clothes.

[P133]
So he had clung to the man, demanding to know where they had come from and begging for a name.

[P134]
After a long struggle, he got the answer he wanted.

[P135]
“From that day on, I vowed that if the Jin Family of Taiyuan ever needed me, I would give this worthless life of mine.”

[P136]
“…!”

[P137]
“And I’m not the only one. Every person here has received help from the Jin Family of Taiyuan, large or small.”

[P138]
Some of those who had received that kindness had left. Others had stayed.

[P139]
And those who stayed were ready to lay down their lives.

[P140]
To protect the land where their fathers and mothers had lived, where they themselves had lived.

[P141]
For the Jin Family of Taiyuan, who had reached out to them when they lay exhausted, waiting to die.

[P142]
That was the Jin Family of Taiyuan’s true strength. It was what had sustained a distinguished family through three hundred years of rises and falls.

[P143]
*Ah.*

[P144]
Wikyung felt an ache deep in his chest.

[P145]
Perhaps he was the one who had underestimated the Jin Family of Taiyuan—and Shanxi Province—most of all.

[P146]
He turned away to hide his reddened eyes.

[P147]
*Thududududu!*

[P148]
Hooves pounded fiercely, their sound clear even from far away.

[P149]
A fine horse raced across the gorge as though something were chasing it. Hanging from the horse was a martial artist of the Jin Family of Taiyuan, dead with his eyes wide open.

[P150]
“…!”

[P151]
“…!”

[P152]
The air froze. Wikyung shouted as though the words were tearing out of him.

[P153]
“Everyone, prepare for battle!”

[P154]
They were here.

# Translation Rules

## Fidelity

- Translate the Korean source—not the wiki, manhwa, fan translations, or expected plot.
- Semantic fidelity outranks elegance. Never improve rhythm, humor, or localization by changing a physical action, negation, relationship, hierarchy, mechanism, quantity, or causal detail.
- Preserve every fact, causal link, joke, emotional beat, repetition, and intentional omission. Add nothing.
- Preserve small action verbs and pragmatic cues exactly: nodding versus shaking one's head, pretending nothing happened, and mild or approachable impressions are characterization, not expendable texture.
- Preserve viewpoint and tense. Resolve omitted subjects only when context supports it; retain genuine ambiguity.
- Match each speaker's hierarchy, intimacy, humor, and profanity naturally. Do not mechanically retain every honorific or classical self-reference.
- Do not censor or soften content.

## Terminology

- `compendium.md` and `docs/NAMES.md` are binding for established names, titles, ranks, techniques, organizations, system terms, items, and locations. Profile headings and aliases join that ledger.
- Search only exact Korean terms already present in the current chapter; the compendium contains future-sensitive entries.
- Never re-romanize established names or invent grand names for uncertain terms. First use of an unlisted name or title almost always needs a footnote or a mapped ledger term.
- Use `qi` for Murim energy and `mana` for the modern Hunter system when the source distinguishes them. Preserve an established chapter-specific rendering such as `internal energy` when the exact glossary and surrounding Korean distinguish accumulated `공력` from resulting `기운`.
- In System panels, render `등급` as `**Grade:**` for quest, item, skill, and martial-art classifications. Reserve `rank` for Hunter classifications or ordinary prose; never replace a System `Grade` field with `Rank`.

## English and Markdown

- Use contemporary US English and natural action-comedy prose; avoid Korean syntax calques and generic cultivation MTL phrasing.
- File: `translations/NNNN.md`; heading: `# Chapter N`.
- Speech: curly double quotes. Direct thoughts: italics without quotes.
- Use em dashes without spaces, the ellipsis character `…`, and `* * *` for source scene breaks.
- Format each actual game System-message panel as one Markdown blockquote window headed `> **System**`. Keep all consecutive notices, fields, and lines inside that same blockquote; separate windows when prose intervenes. Do not enclose System notices or UI terms in square brackets; the `System` heading and framed blockquote identify the panel. Do not label manuals, ordinary quotations, warnings printed in a manual, or other non-System material as `System`; use a normal blockquote or a specific heading instead. Do not wrap each complete notice in outer `**`; retain bold only for meaningful labels or emphasis inside the panel.
- Keep the final file English-only reading copy: no audit notes, Korean text, summaries, or model metadata.

### Tone and Style

- Write like a polished commercial webnovel: brisk, vivid, accessible, and easy to read aloud.
- Preserve the series’ contrast between danger and comedy. Let absurdity, bad timing, blunt reactions, and grim situations create dark humor without adding jokes absent from the Korean.
- Jin Taekyung’s narration is conversational, observant, self-mocking, and occasionally profane. It may be irreverent even when the situation is serious.
- Keep deadpan punchlines short and well-timed. Do not explain a joke after delivering it.
- Preserve the source's level of explicitness. A euphemism may remain euphemistic even when its meaning is sexual or crude; do not replace it with more graphic English merely for impact.
- Make dialogue spontaneous and character-specific. Preserve hierarchy and intimacy through word choice, address, rhythm, and restraint—not archaic wuxia English.
- Use strong profanity when the Korean is strong, but neither intensify nor sanitize it. Do not make ordinary lines uniformly vulgar. Profanity should reveal mood or relationship.
- Keep action and injury vivid but clear rather than purple. Do not make violence funny unless the source’s framing does.
- Avoid stiff literalism, translator-added melodrama, dated internet slang, and quippy superhero-style banter.
- On the second pass, correct awkward English collocations and word choices without changing meaning or voice. Prefer ordinary, spoken English over stiff Latinate or ceremonial wording when the scene is brisk or comic: “goose bumps” rather than “gooseflesh,” and “laid into them” rather than “launched into a solemn denunciation.” Read the prose aloud and replace any phrase that sounds like a formal essay, legal document, or literal dictionary gloss unless the source deliberately calls for that register.

Use `[^1]` Markdown footnotes when a brief, factual, spoiler-free explanation materially helps an English reader understand:

- a Korean institution, living arrangement, food, holiday, myth, historical reference, or local custom;
- a Korean word, phrase, idiom, wordplay, or culturally specific image that cannot be conveyed fully by the best natural English analogy;

At the far end of the vase-shaped gorge, which had swallowed countless lives from the Great Faction War to the present day, stood five towers where none had stood before.

[P71]
Built of mud, wood, and stone, each rose three *jang* high. Each had a level platform large enough to hold a little over two hundred people.

[P72]
Two hundred archers, to be exact.

[P73]
“Taking the heights above the gorge isn’t enough. These forts are essential to victory. Please do everything you can to make sure they don’t collapse.”

[P74]
“Of course, sir.”

[P75]
The old carpenter answered in a folksy drawl.

[P76]
Even as the two spoke, countless people around them went about their assigned tasks.

[P77]
They came from all walks of life.

[P78]
Martial artists in uniforms bearing the names of their sects hauled weapons and heavy materials without pause. Government troops in official uniforms moved at their officers’ commands.

[P79]
But Wikyung’s gaze settled on another group, people dressed in all sorts of clothes with no affiliation to mark them, working just as hard.

[P80]
“Pull on three!”

[P81]
“One, twooo!”

[P82]
“Hyaah!”

[P83]
Men covered in dust kept up the grueling labor, sweat pouring off them.

[P84]
“Where should we put these arrows?”

[P85]
“Oil! Bring the oil over here!”

[P86]
Women carried supplies for the battle and prepared simple food.

[P87]
Looking at the thousands of commoners, Wikyung felt a tightness in his chest.

[P88]
*I told them to flee as far away as they could.*

[P89]
He had warned them sincerely, again and again. He had tried to persuade them.

[P90]
This wasn’t merely a dispute among martial artists.

[P91]
It was a brutal war that would claim countless lives, and they, with no strength to defend themselves, would suffer the most.

[P92]
But they had made up their minds and refused to leave.

[P93]
They had even come to help here, on a battlefield that would soon be swept by bloodshed.

[P94]
Like the old carpenter standing before him.

[P95]
“Looks like our Lesser Family Head has a lot on his mind.”

[P96]
The old carpenter glanced sideways at Wikyung and chuckled.

[P97]
He had passed seventy several years ago. When he laughed, air whistled through the gaps between the few teeth he had left.

[P98]
“Don’t you worry about it. This old man and all those folks came knowing what we were getting into.”

[P99]
“But still… how could I not worry?”

[P100]
“Goodness, please don’t speak so formally to me. I may be an old man without much time left, but I’m not shameless enough to expect honorifics from the Lesser Family Head.”

[P101]
The old carpenter hurriedly waved his hands. Warmth shone in his pale gray eyes as he looked at Wikyung.

[P102]
“Even a beast that can’t speak will repay a kindness someday. How could people turn their backs at a time like this?”

[P103]
“What do you mean…?”

[P104]
“When I was young and full of life, you’d have thought the country was falling apart. The Demonic Cult, or demons, or whatever those wretches were, stirred up trouble everywhere. Then came years of famine.”

[P105]
It had happened long ago, before Jin Wikyung was born.

[P106]
But the old carpenter remembered it clearly: boiling leather to eat and stripping bark from trees to chew.

[P107]
Everyone was starving. There was no one they could ask for help, and no one able to give it.

[P108]
If a group of men hadn’t come to their village one day under the blazing sun, he and his family would have starved to death before long.

[P109]
*“Is this Hong Family Village?”*

[P110]
*“Y-yes, it is. What brings you here…?”*

[P111]
*“Phew. Thank goodness we found the right place.”*

[P112]
What was the point of tilling fields that yielded not a single grain?

[P113]
They had abandoned the barren land long before, gone into the mountains, and become slash-and-burn farmers.

[P114]
So at first, they had thought the newcomers were bandits.

[P115]
Or men sent by someone powerful to squeeze the last drops from people who had neither an iron coin nor a handful of grain left.

[P116]
Why else would anyone come this deep into the mountains?

[P117]
But instead of drawing the swords at their waists, the men set down the loads on their backs.

[P118]
They were huge sacks.

[P119]
Dozens of them, filled with grain and meat—the sight of which had grown so distant he could barely remember it.

[P120]
*“W-what in the world is this…?”*

[P121]
*“Get in line. We’ll hand it out in order.”*

[P122]
It felt like a dream.

[P123]
It still felt like one when everyone in the village lined up as the men instructed, and when he watched his wife and children, who had lain weak and helpless for days, eat until their bellies were full to bursting.

[P124]
Only after staring at that unbelievable sight and swallowing a mouthful of warm meat broth did he realize it was real.

[P125]
So he cried.

[P126]
No—everyone cried.

[P127]
They wept aloud even as they chewed and swallowed the food in their mouths.

[P128]
Because they wanted to live. Because they wanted to know they were alive.

[P129]
“If they hadn’t helped us that day, this old man and my family would have starved to death there.”

[P130]
The old carpenter looked at Wikyung with tears in his eyes. Unlike back then, he had a broad smile on his face.

[P131]
“But those good people tried to leave without a word. So I grabbed one of them by the leg and hung on.”

[P132]
He couldn’t read, not even the writing on their clothes.

[P133]
So he had clung to the man, demanding to know where they had come from and begging for a name.

[P134]
After a long struggle, he got the answer he wanted.

[P135]
“From that day on, I vowed that if the Jin Family of Taiyuan ever needed me, I would give this worthless life of mine.”

[P136]
“…!”

[P137]
“And I’m not the only one. Every person here has received help from the Jin Family of Taiyuan, large or small.”

[P138]
Some of those who had received that kindness had left. Others had stayed.

[P139]
And those who stayed were ready to lay down their lives.

[P140]
To protect the land where their fathers and mothers had lived, where they themselves had lived.

[P141]
For the Jin Family of Taiyuan, who had reached out to them when they lay exhausted, waiting to die.

[P142]
That was the Jin Family of Taiyuan’s true strength. It was what had sustained a distinguished family through three hundred years of rises and falls.

[P143]
*Ah.*

[P144]
Wikyung felt an ache deep in his chest.

[P145]
Perhaps he was the one who had underestimated the Jin Family of Taiyuan—and Shanxi Province—most of all.

[P146]
He turned away to hide his reddened eyes.

[P147]
*Thududududu!*

[P148]
Hooves pounded fiercely, their sound clear even from far away.

[P149]
A fine horse raced across the gorge as though something were chasing it. Hanging from the horse was a martial artist of the Jin Family of Taiyuan, dead with his eyes wide open.

[P150]
“…!”

[P151]
“…!”

[P152]
The air froze. Wikyung shouted as though the words were tearing out of him.

[P153]
“Everyone, prepare for battle!”

[P154]
They were here.

## Critical binding translation rules

# Translation Rules

## Fidelity

- Translate the Korean source—not the wiki, manhwa, fan translations, or expected plot.
- Semantic fidelity outranks elegance. Never improve rhythm, humor, or localization by changing a physical action, negation, relationship, hierarchy, mechanism, quantity, or causal detail.
- Preserve every fact, causal link, joke, emotional beat, repetition, and intentional omission. Add nothing.
- Preserve small action verbs and pragmatic cues exactly: nodding versus shaking one's head, pretending nothing happened, and mild or approachable impressions are characterization, not expendable texture.
- Preserve viewpoint and tense. Resolve omitted subjects only when context supports it; retain genuine ambiguity.
- Match each speaker's hierarchy, intimacy, humor, and profanity naturally. Do not mechanically retain every honorific or classical self-reference.
- Do not censor or soften content.

## Terminology

- `compendium.md` and `docs/NAMES.md` are binding for established names, titles, ranks, techniques, organizations, system terms, items, and locations. Profile headings and aliases join that ledger.
- Search only exact Korean terms already present in the current chapter; the compendium contains future-sensitive entries.
- Never re-romanize established names or invent grand names for uncertain terms. First use of an unlisted name or title almost always needs a footnote or a mapped ledger term.
- Use `qi` for Murim energy and `mana` for the modern Hunter system when the source distinguishes them. Preserve an established chapter-specific rendering such as `internal energy` when the exact glossary and surrounding Korean distinguish accumulated `공력` from resulting `기운`.
- In System panels, render `등급` as `**Grade:**` for quest, item, skill, and martial-art classifications. Reserve `rank` for Hunter classifications or ordinary prose; never replace a System `Grade` field with `Rank`.

## English and Markdown

- Use contemporary US English and natural action-comedy prose; avoid Korean syntax calques and generic cultivation MTL phrasing.
- File: `translations/NNNN.md`; heading: `# Chapter N`.
- Speech: curly double quotes. Direct thoughts: italics without quotes.
- Use em dashes without spaces, the ellipsis character `…`, and `* * *` for source scene breaks.
- Format each actual game System-message panel as one Markdown blockquote window headed `> **System**`. Keep all consecutive notices, fields, and lines inside that same blockquote; separate windows when prose intervenes. Do not enclose System notices or UI terms in square brackets; the `System` heading and framed blockquote identify the panel. Do not label manuals, ordinary quotations, warnings printed in a manual, or other non-System material as `System`; use a normal blockquote or a specific heading instead. Do not wrap each complete notice in outer `**`; retain bold only for meaningful labels or emphasis inside the panel.
- Keep the final file English-only reading copy: no audit notes, Korean text, summaries, or model metadata.

### Tone and Style

- Write like a polished commercial webnovel: brisk, vivid, accessible, and easy to read aloud.
- Preserve the series’ contrast between danger and comedy. Let absurdity, bad timing, blunt reactions, and grim situations create dark humor without adding jokes absent from the Korean.
- Jin Taekyung’s narration is conversational, observant, self-mocking, and occasionally profane. It may be irreverent even when the situation is serious.
- Keep deadpan punchlines short and well-timed. Do not explain a joke after delivering it.
- Preserve the source's level of explicitness. A euphemism may remain euphemistic even when its meaning is sexual or crude; do not replace it with more graphic English merely for impact.
- Make dialogue spontaneous and character-specific. Preserve hierarchy and intimacy through word choice, address, rhythm, and restraint—not archaic wuxia English.
- Use strong profanity when the Korean is strong, but neither intensify nor sanitize it. Do not make ordinary lines uniformly vulgar. Profanity should reveal mood or relationship.
- Keep action and injury vivid but clear rather than purple. Do not make violence funny unless the source’s framing does.
- Avoid stiff literalism, translator-added melodrama, dated internet slang, and quippy superhero-style banter.
- On the second pass, correct awkward English collocations and word choices without changing meaning or voice. Prefer ordinary, spoken English over stiff Latinate or ceremonial wording when the scene is brisk or comic: “goose bumps” rather than “gooseflesh,” and “laid into them” rather than “launched into a solemn denunciation.” Read the prose aloud and replace any phrase that sounds like a formal essay, legal document, or literal dictionary gloss unless the source deliberately calls for that register.

## Footnotes

Use `[^1]` Markdown footnotes when a brief, factual, spoiler-free explanation materially helps an English reader understand:

- a Korean institution, living arrangement, food, holiday, myth, historical reference, or local custom;
- a Korean word, phrase, idiom, wordplay, or culturally specific image that cannot be conveyed fully by the best natural English analogy;
- a deliberately literal rendering whose cultural or linguistic force would otherwise be lost.

For example, render `고시원` as “goshiwon” when the setting or connotations matter, with a concise footnote explaining that it is a very small, inexpensive room-for-rent housing arrangement. Footnotes must be rare, useful, and non-spoiling; do not footnote ordinary vocabulary, fully preserved jokes, or uncertainty. Record consequential uncertainty in `docs/STATE.md`.

- Future knowledge may prevent contradiction but may not add early names, pronouns, certainty, motives, or foreshadowing.

Do not label manuals, ordinary quotations, warnings printed in a manual, or other non-System material as `System`; use a normal blockquote or a specific heading instead. Do not wrap each complete notice in outer `**`; retain bold only for meaningful labels or emphasis inside the panel.

### Tone and Style

- Write like a polished commercial webnovel: brisk, vivid, accessible, and easy to read aloud.
- Preserve the series’ contrast between danger and comedy. Let absurdity, bad timing, blunt reactions, and grim situations create dark humor without adding jokes absent from the Korean.
- Jin Taekyung’s narration is conversational, observant, self-mocking, and occasionally profane. It may be irreverent even when the situation is serious.
- Keep deadpan punchlines short and well-timed. Do not explain a joke after delivering it.
- Preserve the source's level of explicitness. A euphemism may remain euphemistic even when its meaning is sexual or crude; do not replace it with more graphic English merely for impact.
- Make dialogue spontaneous and character-specific. Preserve hierarchy and intimacy through word choice, address, rhythm, and restraint—not archaic wuxia English.
- Use strong profanity when the Korean is strong, but neither intensify nor sanitize it. Do not make ordinary lines uniformly vulgar. Profanity should reveal mood or relationship.
- Keep action and injury vivid but clear rather than purple. Do not make violence funny unless the source’s framing does.
- Avoid stiff literalism, translator-added melodrama, dated internet slang, and quippy superhero-style banter.
- On the second pass, correct awkward English collocations and word choices without changing meaning or voice. Prefer ordinary, spoken English over stiff Latinate or ceremonial wording when the scene is brisk or comic: “goose bumps” rather than “gooseflesh,” and “laid into them” rather than “launched into a solemn denunciation.” Read the prose aloud and replace any phrase that sounds like a formal essay, legal document, or literal dictionary gloss unless the source deliberately calls for that register.

Use `[^1]` Markdown footnotes when a brief, factual, spoiler-free explanation materially helps an English reader understand:

- a Korean institution, living arrangement, food, holiday, myth, historical reference, or local custom;
- a Korean word, phrase, idiom, wordplay, or culturally specific image that cannot be conveyed fully by the best natural English analogy;
- a deliberately literal rendering whose cultural or linguistic force would otherwise be lost.

For example, render `고시원` as “goshiwon” when the setting or connotations matter, with a concise footnote explaining that it is a very small, inexpensive room-for-rent housing arrangement. Prefer the best natural English analogy in the prose. Use a literal translation plus a concise footnote when the Korean wording itself matters. Define a term at its first meaningful occurrence and do not repeat the note unnecessarily. Footnotes must be rare, useful, and non-spoiling; do not footnote ordinary vocabulary, fully preserved jokes, or uncertainty. Record consequential uncertainty in `docs/STATE.md`.
